Deserve
deh-ZERV
v.t. (to merit, by services or conduct; to be worthy of reward or punishment)
Latin deservire, to serve zealously, from de-, thoroughly, and servire, to serve. To deserve is, at root, to have served thoroughly enough to have earned a due return, whether of reward or of penalty.

Biblical Definition

Ezra's great confessional prayer, offered on behalf of the returned exiles after discovering their intermarriage with the surrounding nations, contains the Authorized Version's single use of this word, set inside a remarkable admission of undeserved mercy: after all that is come upon us for our evil deeds, and for our great trespass, seeing that thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve, and hast given us such deliverance as this. Ezra does not plead that the exile and its sufferings were disproportionate; he states, as the premise of his whole prayer, that even the worst that had already fallen on Israel was less than what her iniquities genuinely deserved.

The confession is the opposite of the self-justifying instinct that measures suffering against merit and finds the accounting unfair. Ezra's arithmetic runs the other direction: whatever calamity Israel has actually endured is a mercy, calculated against a true deserving that would have warranted far worse, and the return from exile itself, the deliverance he is praying about, is likewise undeserved on any accounting of Israel's own conduct. A word most often used to demand what is owed to oneself is here used to confess how much worse than what one has already received would actually have been owed, and the whole prayer that follows is built on that reversal.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to merit or be worthy of, by service, conduct, or qualities, either good or bad; to earn by desert.

expand to see more

DESERVE, v.t. To merit; to be worthy of, whether reward or punishment, by one's actions or character.

TRESPASS, n. An offense; a transgression of duty, law, or the rights of another.

INIQUITY, n. Injustice; wickedness; gross violation of right or duty.

DELIVERANCE, n. The act of delivering or freeing; rescue from bondage, danger, or evil.

CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment of a fact, especially of guilt or sin; a public or private admission of wrongdoing.

Key Scripture

Ezr 9:6 — "And said, O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens."

Ezr 9:13 — "And after all that is come upon us for our evil deeds, and for our great trespass, seeing that thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve, and hast given us such deliverance as this;"

Ezr 9:15 — "O LORD God of Israel, thou art righteous: for we remain yet escaped, as it is this day: behold, we are before thee in our trespasses: for we cannot stand before thee because of this."

Lam 3:22 — "It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not."

Modern Corruption

Deserving is invoked mainly to argue that one's suffering is unfair or excessive, when Ezra's own prayer uses the word to confess the opposite - that even severe judgment fell short of what was actually deserved.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; deserve still names what is merited by conduct. The principle worth recovering is the direction Ezra's confession runs. A natural instinct, faced with exile and loss, is to calculate whether the punishment fit the crime and to argue, if possible, that it did not; Ezra instead does the opposite math, insisting that the LORD hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve.

Lamentations supplies the doctrine that makes such a confession bearable rather than merely despairing: it is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. Ezra's prayer and Jeremiah's lament together model a use of the word deserve almost opposite to its ordinary employment — not a demand for what is owed to the speaker, but an honest acknowledgment of how much worse than what has already been received would, by the speaker's own admission, have been entirely just.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chasak (H2820), to withhold, to spare; the verb underlying the idiom “punished us less than,” literally withheld beneath our iniquities, in Ezra 9:13.

expand to see more

Hebrew chasak (H2820) — to withhold, to spare, to keep back; the verb behind the Hebrew idiom rendered “punished us less than our iniquities deserve,” literally withheld beneath.

Hebrew avon (H5771) — iniquity, guilt, punishment for iniquity; the noun measuring what was actually deserved.

Hebrew ma'al (H4604) — a trespass, an unfaithful act; the specific offense, intermarriage with the nations, confessed in Ezra 9.

Hebrew tsaddiq (H6662) — righteous, just; the title Ezra gives the LORD in 9:15 even while confessing Israel's own guilt.

Hebrew checed (H2617) — steadfast covenant love, mercy; the quality Lamentations 3:22 credits for Israel's survival at all.

Usage

"“thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve” — Ezra's confession of undeserved mercy."

"“we are before thee in our trespasses: for we cannot stand before thee” — the honest ground of the whole prayer."

"“It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed” — the same principle from Lamentations."
